newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. landmine move seen blocked at arms talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. landmine move seen blocked at arms talks.

text.p: A United States decision to push for a global ban on land mines at the United Nations-sponsored Geneva Conference on Disarmament (CD) is unlikely to make much immediate headway, diplomats said on Saturday.

They said the U.S. idea, long promoted by fellow nuclear powers Britain and France, would run up against determination among developing countries to drive for a total nuclear disarmament before all else.
"There is not much chance of any quick agreement on this being discussed," said one senior diplomat closely involved in preparations for the CD's first 1997 session due to start up next week.

The so-called Group of 21 of non-aligned countries, with India at the helm, are also refusing to consider another key issue on the nuclear powers' agenda -- negotiation of a cut-off date for production of fissile nuclear material.

India, which almost sunk CD negotiations on a total nuclear test ban treaty (CTBT) last year with a similar demand, is insisting that top of the 61-member body's 1997 agenda should be negotiating a nuclear disarmament agreement.

This is strongly opposed by all five declared nuclear powers -- the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France -- who argue that this can only be handled through bilateral or plurilateral discussions among them.
The widely-differing positions have created an impasse in informal contacts over the past few weeks on what exactly should be on the CD's work programme into the spring.

"The non-aligned are saying that nothing is going to happen before the CD sets up an ad-hoc committee on the elimination of nuclear weapons with the purpose of shaping a treaty within a time-bound framework," said one envoy.
"So it looks as though we are in for several more weeks of discussion and contacts before we know what is going to emerge."

The United States, one of the world's major producers of the some 100 million landmines sown around the world which kill or maim an estimated 25,000 civilians a year, said on Friday it would observe a unilateral ban on their export.
This would bring it into line with several other powers who have already taken similar measures.

At the same time, a spokesman for President Bill Clinton said Washington would seek to start up talks on a global ban -- fiercely advocated by the Geneva-based International Committee of the Red Cross -- when the CD meets next week.

The move would mean sidelining the so-called "Ottawa process" promoted by the Canadian government, which has taken a lead on the issue. A 50-nation conference in Canada's capital last October called for for an early global ban.

Canada, a member of the CD, has gone a step further, proposing work among the 50 to shape a treaty banning the weapons during this year culminating in another Ottawa conference in December to sign it.

But Russia and China, the two top mine producers and exporters, reject this approach. China in particular wants a much more gradual process and kept away from Ottawa. Russia says no credible alternative has yet been found to land mines.
However, diplomats from the other three nuclear powers say both countries have indicated they would be ready for discussions in the CD. "This makes it a much more realistic approach," one envoy said.
